name: Shoe lifts / elevator shoes
lead: Shoe lifts are inserts that raise the heel inside a shoe, and elevator shoes are footwear with a thickened insole or hidden lift that makes the wearer appear taller. Unlike visibly high-heeled shoes, the height-adding component is concealed inside the shoe. Lifts may be made of plastic, rubber, wood or silicone. [1][2]
Thickened soles and heel lifts are also used in orthopedics to compensate for differences in leg length, although the term elevator shoe is not usually applied to those. [1][3][4]

The height gain from a lift equals its thickness and lasts only while the shoe is worn. Clinical research on heel lifts concerns leg-length inequality and associated pain; a 2022 Cochrane review addressed shoe and heel lifts for leg-length inequality in adults with musculoskeletal conditions. One small trial has examined balance with insoles of 3, 5 and 7 cm. [2][3][4]
infobox: Roughly 2-3 cm (inserts) to about 7 cm (built-in lifts)

paras: An elevator shoe has a thickened section under the heel inside the shoe to raise the wearer. The insert version can be placed in ordinary shoes. The lift material may be plastic, wood or rubber, similar to the construction of a platform shoe's heel. [1]
No clinical trial has tested elevator shoes as an appearance product. Related research concerns lifts used for medical reasons and balance with height insoles.

A 2022 Cochrane systematic review examined shoe and heel lifts for leg-length inequality in adults with musculoskeletal conditions. [3] A 2020 study examined orthotic insoles, gait kinematics and low-back pain in patients with mild leg-length discrepancy. [4]

A 2016 randomized study of 30 young adults wore height-adjustable silicone insoles of 3, 5 and 7 cm three times a week for four weeks. The group that also did a program of ankle stretching, strengthening and balance exercises improved balance at all three insole heights compared with the control group, and the authors concluded ankle exercises help prevent ankle joint damage. [2]

The 2016 balance study was framed around ankle joint damage prevention, indicating that raised insoles alter ankle balance demands. [2] Orthopedic literature on lifts concerns gait and pain in people with real leg-length differences, and its findings do not directly address cosmetic use by people with equal leg lengths. [3][4]

Height is a frequently discussed attribute in appearance communities, and lifts are used as an immediate, reversible way to add apparent height of a few centimetres. The effect disappears when the shoes are removed.
